trap.why: Most changes can be additive with no version at all. Frequent versions multiply what you support forever.
trap.probe: Additive by default, a clear definition of breaking, per-version telemetry, translation at the edge.
trap.say: "Additive changes need no version; a breaking change gets a new version translated at the edge, with a dated support policy and usage telemetry per client."

thesis: Make additive change the default so most changes need no new version at all, reserve explicit versions for genuinely breaking changes, and back every version with a published support policy, per-version usage telemetry and contract tests. You can't force clients, so make staying compatible cheap and moving forward easy.
pitch: Most API evolution should be additive: new optional fields, new endpoints, new optional parameters, with clients required to ignore unknown fields, so nothing breaks and nothing needs a version bump. For breaking changes, like removing or renaming fields, changing types or semantics, or changing error behaviour, I'd introduce an explicit version, either in the path like /v2 or in a header or dated version like Stripe's, and keep the old one working. Each version has a published support policy with dates. I'd measure usage per version and per client, so deprecation decisions are data-driven and I can contact the clients still on old versions. Contract tests, from consumer-driven contracts or recorded real traffic, catch accidental breaks before release. Internally, translating old versions into the current model at the edge keeps the core code from forking per version.

points.d: New optional fields and endpoints don't break well-behaved clients. Document that clients must ignore unknown fields and tolerate new enum values.
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or formats, making optional inputs required, changing defaults, semantics or error codes. Publish the list.
Path versions (/v2) are visible and simple; header or date-based versions (pin each client to the version at signup) allow finer-grained evolution. Be consistent.
Keep one current internal model; adapters convert old request and response shapes. This avoids parallel codebases per version.
How long each version is supported after its successor ships, communicated in docs and changelogs.
Track calls by version and client id. You can't deprecate safely without knowing who still depends on what.
Consumer-driven contracts or tests replaying real requests verify that changes don't break existing clients.

decision: Additive changes with no version bump whenever possible. A new version only for unavoidable breaking changes, with translation adapters, a dated support window, and telemetry-driven deprecation.
numbers: Support window example: a minimum of 12 months after a successor is available for external APIs, longer for mobile apps with slow upgrade curves.
pitfalls: Bumping the version for every change, multiplying versions to support.
Silent semantic changes within a version (same field, different meaning).
No per-client usage data, so deprecation is guesswork.
Forking the codebase per version instead of translating at the edge.

followups.a: Path is easier to see, cache and route; header or date-based versioning suits APIs with frequent small changes and lets each client pin. Either works if applied consistently.

followups.q: How do you handle mobile apps that never update?
followups.a: Long support windows, server-side translation for old versions, minimum-version enforcement only for security-critical cases, with in-app upgrade prompts.

followups.q: How do you change an enum safely?
followups.a: Add values as a documented possibility; clients must handle unknown values. Never repurpose an existing value.

example: A payments API pins each integration to the API version current at signup. Breaking changes ship as new dated versions; a translation layer converts responses for older versions. Usage dashboards show which merchants are on each version, and the team contacts the long tail before retiring anything.
